faqs.a: A half-life is the time needed for half of a substance to decay or disappear. After one half-life, 50% remains; after two, 25%; after three, 12.5%. The amount never truly hits zero - it halves forever.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years. Measuring how much C-14 remains in an ancient sample tells archaeologists how many half-lives have passed, and therefore how old the sample is.
faqs.q: How is half-life used in carbon dating?

faqs.a: No. Half-life assumes a constant decay rate. Real systems can have multiple decay paths, environmental effects, or changing conditions. It is an excellent model for ideal exponential decay, not a guarantee about the real world.
faqs.q: Is everything with a half-life perfectly predictable?

faqs.a: Divide the elapsed time by the half-life: n = t / t(1/2). For 15 hours elapsed and a 5-hour half-life, n = 3 half-lives. The remaining amount is then the initial amount times (1/2)^n.
faqs.q: How do I find the number of half-lives?

faqs.a: They never do, in theory. Halving 1 gives 0.5, then 0.25, then 0.125, and so on - always some tiny amount left. In practice, scientists treat amounts below detection limits as zero.
faqs.q: Does the amount ever reach zero?

faqs.a: No. The half-life is a property of the process, not the amount. Whether you start with 100 grams or 1 gram, half disappears in one half-life. That is what makes the concept so powerful.
faqs.q: Does starting with more change the half-life?

half-life-calculator.formula:
Remaining = initial x (1/2)^(elapsed / half-life)
Number of half-lives n = elapsed / half-life.
Decayed = initial - remaining.
howTo: Enter the starting amount of your substance.
Enter its half-life and pick the time unit (seconds to years).
Enter how much time has passed, in the same unit.
Read the remaining amount, the decayed amount, and how many half-lives passed.
Try the carbon-14 example: half-life 5,730 years, to date ancient samples.
keyFacts: A half-life is the time for exactly half of a quantity to decay.
After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)^n of the original.
Decay is exponential: the rate of loss is proportional to the amount present.
The half-life does not depend on the starting amount.
Common half-lives: carbon-14 is 5,730 years, uranium-238 is 4.5 billion years, technetium-99m is 6 hours.
The formula also describes drug elimination, capacitor discharge, and population decline.

half-life-calculator.quickAnswer: Starting with 100 grams of a substance whose half-life is 5 hours, after 15 hours exactly 3 half-lives have passed. Each half-life cuts the amount in half: 100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5 grams. So 12.5 grams remain and 87.5 grams have decayed. The formula is: remaining = initial x (1/2)^(elapsed / half-life).
half-life-calculator.tagline: Compute what remains after exponential decay - any substance, any time unit.
half-life-calculator.workedExample:
100 grams, half-life 5 hours, elapsed 15 hours:
1. Number of half-lives: n = 15 / 5 = 3.
2. Remaining fraction: (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 0.125.
3. Remaining: 100 x 0.125 = 12.5 grams.
4. Decayed: 100 - 12.5 = 87.5 grams.
5. Percent remaining: 12.5%.
